blocks.md: An indicator, or dummy, variable is a yes-or-no switch in a regression: it equals one if an observation belongs to a group — a house in a particular neighbourhood, a worker who is female — and zero otherwise. With a single dummy, the regression simply compares the average outcome of the two groups: the intercept is the average for the zero group, and the dummy's coefficient is the gap between the groups. Several categories need one dummy fewer than the number of categories.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Dummies are how regressions handle categories, and reading them as gaps relative to a reference group is essential to interpreting results.
Also called factor or dummy variables. A binary regressor turns the regression into a **comparison of two group means**. That equivalence is the whole section.

blocks.tex: UTOWN = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{house in University Town} \\ 0, & \text{house in Golden Oaks}\end{cases}, \qquad PRICE = \beta_1 + \beta_2\,UTOWN + e

blocks.md: Always write out the regression function for each value of the indicator:
So $\beta_1$ is the mean of the **omitted (reference) group**, and $\beta_2$ is the **difference** in means.

**Proof sketch.** With $x_i\in\{0,1\}$, $\bar{x} = n_1/n$. The denominator of $b_2$ is $n_1 n_0/n$ and the numerator simplifies to $(n_1 n_0/n)(\bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_0)$, so $b_2 = \bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_0$ and $b_1 = \bar{y} - b_2\bar{x} = \bar{y}_0$.

sections.heading: It nests the two-sample t test

blocks.md: Testing $H_0: \beta_2 = 0$ with the usual $t$ statistic is **algebraically identical** to the pooled-variance two-sample $t$ test from elementary statistics. Say that if asked why we bother: regression nests the simpler test as a special case and extends it to controls.
with $\beta_1 = \overline{WAGE}_{Male}$ and $\beta_2 = \overline{WAGE}_{Female} - \overline{WAGE}_{Male}$. Note this is a **raw gap** with no controls — not an estimate of discrimination.

The lecture first plots the two wage distributions (the `cps_small` data, 1,000 workers): both are right-skewed, and the men's is shifted right. Regressing wage on the female indicator gives $\widehat{WAGE} = 11.53 - 2.66\,FEMALE$, so men average \$11.53 an hour and women $11.53 - 2.66 = \$8.87$; the gap has $t = -6.88$. With no other controls this is a raw difference in means, not an estimate of discrimination.

sections.heading: Multiple categories and the dummy variable trap

blocks.md: For $k$ levels, include **$k-1$** dummies plus the intercept:

Including all $k$ alongside an intercept makes the dummy columns sum to the column of ones — perfect multicollinearity, $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}$ singular, no unique solution. That is the **dummy variable trap**, and it is [Full Rank and Identification](note:full-rank-and-identification) made concrete: there exists $\boldsymbol{\delta}\neq\mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\delta} = \mathbf{0}$.
The omitted level is the **reference group**, and every coefficient is read as a difference from it.
Check the counts in each level before estimating. A level with very few observations gives a coefficient with a huge standard error.
